name: When Not to Use AI
title: When Not to Use AI
answer: This idea says that some parts of teaching should stay entirely human, including conversations about student struggles, feedback on deeply personal writing, and decisions about grades or placement. It matters because using AI in those moments can make students feel like a case to be handled rather than a person who is seen, and because AI is a poor fit when accuracy is critical and hard to check. Teachers should decide when AI helps and when it does not.

sections.body: The idea is a boundary for AI use in teaching. It addresses the risk that teachers apply AI to every task simply because it is available. Certain work calls for a teacher's full attention, such as sensitive conversations, personal writing feedback, and grade or placement decisions. AI is also a poor fit when a teacher cannot easily verify its accuracy, because an unfamiliar topic makes errors hard to spot. Certain work deserves a slower pace, and speed is not the goal for every task.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the text does not give grade bands, so the guidance applies across ages. Teachers reserve their own time and voice for conversations with students about their struggles, feedback on deeply personal writing, and decisions about a student's grade or placement. When accuracy is critical and checking is hard, especially on a topic the teacher does not know well, materials the school trusts or a colleague who knows the subject are safer than an AI draft. AI is most useful when the teacher has enough knowledge to notice and correct its errors. For tasks worth doing slowly, such as writing a thoughtful note to a struggling student or planning a lesson the teacher cares deeply about, the teacher may choose to work without AI.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no evidence label, study, figure, or finding for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research. The guidance is presented as professional judgment about when human attention and verification matter most.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that AI can make students feel like a case to be handled rather than a person who is seen, and it can produce errors that a teacher unfamiliar with the topic may not notice. In those cases, materials the school trusts or a colleague who knows the subject are safer. Decisions about a student's grade or placement, feedback on deeply personal writing, and conversations about struggles stay with the teacher. Teachers should have permission to decide when AI is useful and when it is not, and they should not assume every task must be faster. This is practice guidance, not legal advice.
